text:
2. Image acquisition
Probe, windows, and technique for this module.
Use a phased array (cardiac) probe on the cardiac preset. LV function is assessed across multiple windows — no single view is sufficient. The goal is to visualize the LV in two orthogonal planes and assess wall motion in all segments.


Parasternal long axis






Tip






What you are looking for: Global LV contractility (do the walls move vigorously inward in systole?), chamber size (a dilated LV suggests chronicity), and mitral valve excursion (reduced in low-output states). M-mode at the tips of the mitral valve leaflets allows measurement of EPSS (E-point septal separation) — a distance greater than 7 mm suggests reduced EF; greater than 13 mm correlates with severely reduced EF.






Tip









Parasternal short axis — papillary muscle level






Tip






What you are looking for: The LV should appear round in cross-section and contract concentrically and symmetrically. This is the best single view for a visual EF estimate — watch the endocardium sweep inward in systole. Also assess the interventricular septum: a flat or D-shaped LV indicates RV pressure or volume overload (see Module 3).



Apical four-chamber






Tip






What you are looking for: All four chambers, with attention to LV wall motion in each visible segment. The apical view is essential for identifying apical wall motion abnormalities (LAD territory) and for assessing LV size relative to the RV.



Subcostal






Tip






When to use: First-line in the unstable patient who cannot be repositioned. Provides a rapid visual impression of global LV function. Not sufficient alone for wall motion analysis.

title: Module 2 — Left Ventricular Function
text:
3. Visual global assessment
Train your eye by comparing the spectrum of LV function side by side. Use the normal clips as your reference, then scroll through progressively reduced function.


Normal LV function (EF 55–70%)






Tip







Assess inward endocardial motion and systolic myocardial thickening across adequate views. Normal contraction reduces cavity size without requiring near-obliteration. If image quality or interpretation is uncertain, obtain additional views or expert/comprehensive assessment and document the limitation; uncertainty does not establish normal function.



Hyperdynamic LV (EF >70%)






Tip






Near-complete cavity obliteration in systole. Common in sepsis (early), anemia, hyperthyroidism, and hypovolemia. In a hypotensive patient, a hyperdynamic LV points away from cardiogenic shock — consider distributive or hypovolemic etiologies, though mixed shock states are possible.



Mildly to moderately reduced LV (EF 30–54%)






Tip







Wall motion is reduced but clearly present. The LV may or may not be dilated. Does not automatically mean cardiogenic shock — assess for hemodynamic compromise and end-organ perfusion. Common in known heart failure presenting with decompensation. Treat the precipitant: arrhythmia, ischemia, infection, medication non-compliance. Avoid negative inotropes and large fluid boluses.



Severely reduced LV (EF <30%)






Tip








Wall motion and systolic thickening are globally reduced. The LV may be dilated, and EPSS may be increased. Severe dysfunction in a hypotensive patient warrants urgent assessment of perfusion and forward flow, but does not prove that cardiogenic shock is the dominant mechanism. Causes include ischemic or dilated cardiomyopathy, myocarditis, Takotsubo, and sepsis-associated dysfunction. Avoid empiric large fluid loads when congestion is present. Use vasoactive support or mechanical support according to the hemodynamic syndrome and specialist assessment, not EF alone.

title: Module 2 — Left Ventricular Function
text:
4. Regional wall motion abnormalities
Regional myocardial function is assessed by wall thickening and endocardial motion. Segmental dysfunction confined to a coronary territory suggests acute coronary syndrome — the pattern tells you which vessel is involved.


Coronary perfusion territories

The LV is divided into segments that correspond to the three major coronary arteries. On the parasternal short axis at mid-papillary level:

LAD (left anterior descending) — anterior wall, anteroseptal wall, apex
RCA (right coronary artery) — inferior wall, inferoseptal wall
LCx (left circumflex) — lateral wall, inferolateral wall, anterolateral wall

Recognizing which segments are affected tells you which vessel is the culprit — and whether the RV is at risk (RCA territory).



Wall motion scoring
Each segment is graded by wall thickening in systole compared to diastole:








Grade
Motion
Wall thickening




Normal
Normal endocardial inward motion
>40% increase


Hypokinetic
Reduced inward motion
10–40% increase


Akinetic
Absent motion
<10% increase


Dyskinetic
Paradoxical outward motion in systole
Thinning or no thickening



For focused cardiac ultrasound, the goal is to identify major abnormalities — severely hypokinetic, akinetic, or dyskinetic segments — not to formally score every segment.



Anterior wall (LAD territory)






Tip






Anterior and anteroseptal hypokinesis or akinesis on PSAX. On A4C, the apical and septal segments are affected. LAD occlusion produces the largest territory of dysfunction and is the most common cause of cardiogenic shock from acute MI.



Inferior wall (RCA territory)






Tip






Inferior and inferoseptal dysfunction often involves the RCA territory, with variation by coronary anatomy. Assess the RV when inferior RWMA is present. In hypotensive RV infarction, assess preload and congestion before a cautious fluid challenge; reassess immediately and stop if flow or perfusion fails to improve or congestion worsens. Avoid preload-reducing drugs when hypotension or preload dependence is present. Urgent reperfusion remains central.



Lateral wall (LCx territory)






Tip






Anterolateral and inferolateral wall dysfunction on PSAX. On A4C, the lateral wall segments are affected. LCx territory infarcts are often ECG-silent (no ST elevation in standard leads) — bedside echo may be the first clue.



Septal dyskinesis






Tip






Paradoxical septal motion — the septum moves away from the LV cavity in systole instead of toward it. Can be seen after cardiac surgery (post-pericardiotomy), with a left bundle branch block, or with RV pressure overload causing septal shift. Not always ischemic — correlate with the clinical context.



Takotsubo (stress) cardiomyopathy






Tip






Apical and mid-ventricular dysfunction with preserved basal contraction can suggest Takotsubo, especially when the distribution extends beyond a single coronary territory. Basal sparing alone does not distinguish it from distal LAD ischemia, and other Takotsubo patterns exist. Evaluate ACS appropriately rather than excluding it from the echo pattern. Stress history is supportive, not diagnostic. Recovery is common, but acute complications, including shock, require assessment. International consensus.

title: Module 2 — Left Ventricular Function
text:
5. Integration cases
Cases where the finding changes management.


Case 1: Hypotension after STEMI
Clinical scenario: A 61-year-old man with an anterior STEMI is brought to the ED. He received aspirin and heparin in the field. On arrival his BP is 78/50, HR 110, and he is cool and diaphoretic. The cath lab team is being activated.
What exam would you perform? Rapid focused cardiac ultrasound before transfer to the cath lab.






Tip






What you see: Severely reduced EF. Anterior and apical wall akinesis. LV not markedly dilated (acute presentation). No pericardial effusion.
How does this change management? The supplied STEMI and hypoperfusion make MI-related cardiogenic shock a major concern. Expedite coronary reperfusion and activate the shock team. Support arterial pressure and, if low output persists, consider inotropic support according to hemodynamics. Avoid large empiric fluid boluses. Mechanical support is selected case by case; it is not an automatic consequence of low EF. Do not delay transfer for a prolonged echo.



Case 2: Undifferentiated hypotension in the ICU
Clinical scenario: A 58-year-old woman with septic shock from a urinary source has been on norepinephrine for 18 hours. She received 4 L of crystalloid. Her BP is now 72/40 despite escalating vasopressors. Lactate is rising.
What exam would you perform? Bedside cardiac ultrasound — LV function, RV size, IVC.






Tip








What you see: Severely reduced EF. Global hypokinesis. LV not dilated. IVC is plethoric.
How does this change management? Sepsis-associated myocardial dysfunction may be contributing, but low EF and a plethoric IVC do not establish the dominant shock mechanism. BP 72/40 gives an approximate MAP of 51 mm Hg: continue resuscitation and titrate necessary vasopressor support. Pause further empiric fluid loading while assessing responsiveness and tolerance. Assess forward flow, perfusion, and congestion; obtain comprehensive echo and consider advanced hemodynamic monitoring if uncertainty persists. Inotropes may be appropriate for cardiac dysfunction with persistent hypoperfusion despite adequate volume and arterial pressure, in addition to required vasopressors. Reassess the response promptly after each intervention; a later repeat echo can follow myocardial recovery. SSC 2026.



Case 3: Chest pain and new ECG changes
Clinical scenario: A 49-year-old woman presents with 2 hours of substernal chest pressure and diaphoresis. ECG shows ST depression in V4–V6. She is hemodynamically stable.
What exam would you perform? Focused cardiac ultrasound to assess for RWMA.






Tip






What you see: Lateral wall hypokinesis. Preserved global function. No effusion.
How does this change management? This is suspected high-risk NSTE-ACS. A lateral RWMA supports the concern but may be old and does not alone establish acute infarction. Obtain serial ECGs and high-sensitivity troponin, begin appropriate ACS care, and involve cardiology urgently for risk-based invasive evaluation. Immediate angiography is indicated for qualifying very-high-risk features such as refractory/recurrent ischemia despite treatment, hemodynamic instability, or life-threatening arrhythmia; if present, do not wait for troponin. The stable scenario as written does not establish those features. ESC ACS guideline.



Case 4: Young patient with viral prodrome and shock
Clinical scenario: A 28-year-old man presents with 5 days of viral URI symptoms followed by 24 hours of progressive dyspnea and now hypotension (BP 88/60). He has no cardiac history.
What exam would you perform? Focused cardiac ultrasound.






Tip






What you see: Severely reduced EF. Globally hypokinetic but not dilated LV. No RWMA pattern. Small pericardial effusion.
How does this change management? Suspected fulminant myocarditis with shock. The viral prodrome, global dysfunction, and small effusion support this working diagnosis but do not exclude ACS or other causes. Urgently involve cardiology/the shock team, stabilize pressure and perfusion, and consider mechanical support if needed. CMR can characterize inflammation when feasible; endomyocardial biopsy may be indicated in high-risk or unstable disease when the histological diagnosis changes treatment. Neither diagnostic test should delay resuscitation. ESC 2025.






Tip



Case format reminder: The case ends with a management decision, not just a diagnosis.

title: Module 2 — Left Ventricular Function
text:
Quiz






Note



Q1. A hypotensive patient has a hyperdynamic LV on bedside echo. What does this tell you about the etiology of shock?






Caution





Answer A hyperdynamic appearance makes severe global systolic depression unlikely, but does not establish adequate cardiac output or select a treatment. Consider distributive, hypovolemic, obstructive, and mixed mechanisms; assess stroke volume/forward flow, perfusion, and the rest of the examination. A small LV can eject a high fraction of a small end-diastolic volume.



Q2. What is EPSS, and what does an elevated value indicate?






Caution





Answer E-point septal separation — the distance between the anterior mitral leaflet at its maximum opening excursion (E-point) and the interventricular septum, measured by M-mode on PLAX. Normal is less than 7 mm. Values above 7 mm correlate with reduced EF. It is a useful single-number surrogate when visual estimation is uncertain.



Q3. You see hypokinesis of the inferior wall and posterior wall on PSAX. What coronary territory does this implicate, and what additional structure should you assess?






Caution





Answer Inferior and inferoseptal dysfunction often involves the RCA territory, with variation by coronary anatomy. Assess the RV when inferior RWMA is present. In hypotensive RV infarction, assess preload and congestion before a cautious fluid challenge; reassess immediately and stop if flow or perfusion fails to improve or congestion worsens. Avoid preload-reducing drugs when hypotension or preload dependence is present. Urgent reperfusion remains central.



Q4. A patient has a severely reduced EF with a markedly dilated LV. A second patient has a severely reduced EF with a normal-sized LV. What does the difference in LV size suggest?






Caution





Answer LV dilation supports chronic remodeling such as dilated cardiomyopathy or longstanding ischemic disease, but it does not exclude a new acute insult. A nondilated LV with severe dysfunction raises concern for an acute process such as myocarditis, Takotsubo, or acute MI, but size alone cannot date the dysfunction. Compare prior imaging and integrate the presentation, ECG, biomarkers, perfusion, and a comprehensive examination.



Q5. What is the Takotsubo pattern, and how does it differ from an LAD occlusion on bedside echo?






Caution





Answer A circumferential mid/apical pattern extending beyond one coronary territory raises suspicion for Takotsubo. Basal sparing alone is insufficient: distal LAD occlusion can spare basal myocardium. Integrate the acute presentation, ECG and biomarkers, and appropriate coronary evaluation to exclude ACS; do not diagnose Takotsubo from this pattern alone.

title: Module 4 — Pericardium
text:
What clinical question does this exam answer, and how do findings change management?






Note



The bedside decision frame: Answer three questions in order.

Is there a pericardial effusion? Confirm an echo-free space in at least two views and distinguish it from pleural fluid, fat, and ascites.
Is cardiac filling impaired? Size alone does not determine significance. Integrate right-sided chamber collapse, IVC plethora, Doppler respiratory variation, and the patient’s hemodynamics.
What needs to happen now? An unstable patient with an effusion and tamponade physiology needs immediate specialist activation for drainage. A stable patient may need comprehensive echocardiography, monitoring, and treatment of the cause instead.



POCUS rapidly detects pericardial fluid and signs of hemodynamic effect. It does not diagnose tamponade from effusion size alone, exclude a loculated post-operative collection after one normal window, or establish acute pericarditis by itself. The final interpretation is the combination of ultrasound, physiology, and clinical context.

title: Module 4 — Pericardium
text:
2. Image acquisition
Probe, windows, and technique for this module.
Use a phased array (cardiac) probe on the cardiac preset. Start with the window that is fastest and clearest in the patient in front of you; the subcostal view is often first in an unstable supine patient. PLAX, PSAX, and apical views provide complementary information.
Depth and gain: Keep the entire cardiac silhouette and posterior pericardium on screen with a small margin beyond it. Too little depth can clip a posterior effusion; excessive gain can make simple fluid look echogenic.
Measurement: Describe location and distribution, then measure the largest echo-free separation at end-diastole. The traditional semiquantitative categories are small (<10 mm), moderate (10–20 mm), and large (>20 mm). Record the view and site of measurement rather than treating one number as an estimate of volume.


Subcostal four-chamber






Tip






The RV free wall is nearest the probe. Fan through the entire cardiac silhouette, watching the RA free wall through systole and the RV free wall at the start of diastole. Extend the same window inferiorly to assess the IVC.



Parasternal long axis






Tip






Effusion on PLAX commonly appears as an echo-free stripe posterior to the LV. Key landmark: the descending thoracic aorta in cross-section near the left atrium. Pericardial fluid remains anterior to the descending aorta; left pleural fluid extends posterior to it.



Apical four-chamber






Tip






The apical view helps define circumferential or loculated fluid and shows RA free-wall motion well. Avoid an off-axis view that foreshortens the ventricles or mistakes pleural fluid for pericardial fluid.

title: Module 4 — Pericardium
text:
3. Recognizing effusion and common mimics

Normal pericardium






Tip






A thin, bright (hyperechoic) line surrounds the heart and moves with it. A physiologic trace of fluid can appear as a very thin posterior stripe on PLAX. Do not call a pathologic effusion from one equivocal view.


Pericardial and epicardial fat






Tip






Annotated PLAX example: Bronshteyn et al., Diagnostics 2024 (CC BY 4.0).
Fat is the most common mimic of pericardial fluid. It is usually echogenic or speckled, most prominent anteriorly, and not a uniformly anechoic collection.

A superficial pericardial fat pad is relatively fixed.
Epicardial fat moves with the heart and sits between myocardium and visceral pericardium.
Free-flowing effusion changes distribution with gravity; a loculated effusion may not.




Small effusion






Tip






Less than 10 mm in maximal end-diastolic separation. A small effusion may be visible only posteriorly or in one dependent region.
Teaching points:

Usually does not produce chamber collapse, but a rapidly accumulating or loculated collection can be important despite a small measured width.
Common causes include pericarditis, malignancy, uremia, trauma, and recent procedures.
In a patient with pleuritic chest pain, a new effusion supports acute pericarditis but does not establish the diagnosis on its own.




Moderate to large effusion






Tip






Moderate: 10–20 mm; large: >20 mm at end-diastole. Large free-flowing effusions are often circumferential and visible in several windows.
Teaching points:

A “swinging heart” is a clue to a very large effusion, but chamber collapse and clinical physiology determine urgency.
Size does not equal tamponade. A large chronic effusion may be tolerated because the pericardium has stretched. A rapidly accumulating effusion can cause tamponade at a much smaller volume.
Always assess chamber collapse, IVC, respiratory interaction, and blood pressure when an effusion is present.




Loculated effusion






Tip






Loculated effusions do not distribute freely. They occur after cardiac surgery, trauma, or prior pericarditis with adhesions. The collection may compress only one chamber and produce regional tamponade without the classic pattern.
Teaching points:

A normal subcostal view does not exclude a loculated collection; check all windows.
Echogenic or heterogeneous fluid suggests blood, clot, debris, or exudate.
Obtain urgent comprehensive imaging and specialist input. A loculated collection may require a different drainage route or surgery.




Post-operative appearance
After cardiac surgery, adhesions can produce anterior, loculated, or regional collections. Classic findings may be absent, and TTE windows may be limited. New post-operative hemodynamic instability with an equivocal bedside exam warrants urgent comprehensive echo—often TEE—and surgical evaluation.



Mimics and pitfalls







Mimic
Key distinguishing feature




Left pleural effusion
Extends posterior to the descending aorta on PLAX


Pericardial or epicardial fat
Echogenic or speckled rather than uniformly anechoic; often anterior


Ascites
Lies below the diaphragm and does not surround the heart


Right pleural effusion
Lateral to the RA/RV on subcostal imaging; does not wrap around the heart


Severely dilated coronary sinus
Tubular structure in the posterior AV groove; confirm in orthogonal views and with Doppler

title: Module 4 — Pericardium
text:
4. Tamponade physiology

Tamponade physiology






Tip






Tamponade occurs when pericardial pressure impairs cardiac filling and reduces stroke volume. It is a clinical-hemodynamic diagnosis supported by ultrasound. No single finding is diagnostic in isolation.








Finding
Best view
Interpretation




Pericardial effusion
Any two cardiac views
Required for effusive tamponade; size alone does not define severity


RA free-wall collapse
Subcostal or apical
Often the earliest finding; longer collapse is more specific


RV free-wall collapse in early diastole
PLAX, PSAX, or subcostal
More specific sign of elevated pericardial pressure


Plethoric IVC with reduced inspiratory collapse
Subcostal IVC
Sensitive for elevated RA pressure but nonspecific


Exaggerated respiratory ventricular interaction
PSAX and apical Doppler
>25% mitral E-wave decrease and >40% tricuspid E-wave increase during inspiration in spontaneous breathing




Doppler respiratory variation






Tip






From the apical four-chamber view, place the PW Doppler sample at the mitral leaflet tips and record several respiratory cycles at a slow sweep speed. In spontaneous breathing, tamponade can produce a >25% inspiratory fall in mitral E-wave velocity and a reciprocal >40% inspiratory rise in tricuspid E-wave velocity.
These thresholds are supportive, not standalone diagnostic tests. Atrial fibrillation, tachypnea, high respiratory effort, and positive-pressure ventilation make interpretation less reliable; during positive-pressure ventilation the expected pattern can be blunted or reversed.






Warning



Context can hide classic signs. Pulmonary hypertension or severe RV hypertrophy can prevent right-sided collapse. Hypovolemia can produce low-pressure tamponade without a plethoric IVC. Positive-pressure ventilation alters Doppler respiratory variation. Loculated or post-operative collections may compress only one chamber.


Management implication: In a hemodynamically unstable patient with a compatible effusion and tamponade physiology, activate the team capable of definitive drainage immediately. Pericardiocentesis, surgical drainage, or operative repair depends on cause, location, and local expertise. Use cautious volume or vasopressor support only as a bridge when needed; neither relieves the obstruction. Comprehensive echo is valuable when it can be obtained without delaying source control.

title: Module 4 — Pericardium
text:
5. Integration cases
Cases where the finding changes management.


Case 1: Post-procedure hypotension
Clinical scenario: A 68-year-old man undergoes right heart catheterization for pulmonary hypertension workup. Thirty minutes later he is hypotensive (BP 82/50), tachycardic (HR 118), and diaphoretic.
What exam would you perform? Focused cardiac ultrasound, subcostal view first.






Tip






What you see: Large circumferential effusion. RA free wall collapses in systole. RV collapse begins in early diastole. IVC is 2.4 cm with minimal inspiratory collapse.
How does this change management? Activate interventional cardiology and cardiac surgery immediately and prepare for definitive drainage. Avoid repeated empiric fluid boluses; a cautious bolus or vasopressor may support preload and perfusion only while the drainage team mobilizes. Neither is definitive therapy.



Case 2: Dyspnea in a cancer patient
Clinical scenario: A 54-year-old woman with metastatic lung adenocarcinoma presents with two weeks of worsening exertional dyspnea and chest fullness. BP 104/72, HR 102. JVD is present, and CXR shows an enlarged cardiac silhouette.
What exam would you perform? Focused cardiac ultrasound using subcostal and PLAX views at minimum.






Tip






What you see: Large pericardial effusion in PLAX without visible RV free-wall collapse in this loop. Effusion size alone does not establish tamponade; integrate right-sided chamber behavior in multiple views, IVC findings, Doppler, and the clinical examination.
How does this change management? This large, symptomatic cancer-associated effusion needs urgent comprehensive echocardiography, monitored admission, and oncology/cardiology consultation. Malignant involvement is suspected, not established by cancer history or ultrasound; fluid cytology or tissue may establish the cause, and treatment-related or infectious causes remain possible. Absence of chamber collapse alone does not establish safe discharge. Define a specialist drainage/evaluation plan and reassess promptly if physiology changes.



Case 3: Undifferentiated shock in the ED
Clinical scenario: A 44-year-old man arrives after being found unresponsive. BP 70/40, HR 124, GCS 10. He is cool and mottled with distended neck veins.
What exam would you perform? Immediate focused cardiac ultrasound as part of resuscitation.






Tip






What you see: Moderate effusion. RA collapse is present; RV collapse is not clear because image quality is limited.
How does this change management? Activate the drainage team and treat this as obstructive shock. Avoid unnecessary deep sedation and positive-pressure ventilation because both can reduce venous return and precipitate collapse. If cardiac arrest occurs, continue high-quality resuscitation while the team rapidly relieves tamponade; treat a shockable rhythm when present and address the reversible cause without delay.



Case 4: Dialysis patient with chest pain
Clinical scenario: A 62-year-old man on hemodialysis presents with sharp chest pain worse when lying flat after missing two sessions. Vitals are stable. ECG shows diffuse ST elevation with PR depression.
What exam would you perform? Focused cardiac ultrasound to assess for effusion and tamponade physiology.






Tip






What you see: Small-to-moderate posterior effusion. No chamber collapse. IVC is 2.5 cm, consistent with elevated right atrial pressure in this clinical context.
How does this change management? Suspect uremic pericarditis with a small-to-moderate effusion and no current tamponade. Coordinate urgent nephrology and cardiology evaluation; intensified dialysis is usually first-line when there is no tamponade. Admit for monitoring and repeat imaging. Drainage is required if tamponade develops or the effusion enlarges despite treatment.



Case 5: Thoracic trauma
Clinical scenario: A 29-year-old woman is intubated after a high-speed MVC. BP 88/60 on vasopressors, HR 135. Bilateral breath sounds are present.
What exam would you perform? eFAST with the focused cardiac view prioritized during the resuscitation.






Tip






What you see: Pericardial fluid anterior to the RV with RV diastolic collapse. No pleural fluid is seen.
How does this change management? Hemopericardium with tamponade physiology in an unstable trauma patient requires immediate trauma and cardiothoracic surgical activation; do not delay source control for CT. Pericardiocentesis may be an imperfect bridge when surgical access is delayed because clotted blood may not drain. If arrest occurs, resuscitative thoracotomy is selected according to injury mechanism, signs of life, arrest duration, local protocol, and team capability—not from the ultrasound finding alone.



Case 6: Recurrent chest pain after pericarditis
Clinical scenario: A 35-year-old man treated for acute pericarditis three months ago returns with recurrent pleuritic chest pain and low-grade fever. His prior small effusion resolved on follow-up.
What exam would you perform? Focused cardiac ultrasound to assess for recurrent effusion, tamponade physiology, and LV function.






Tip






What you see: Small posterior effusion. No tamponade physiology. Normal LV function.
How does this change management? Recurrent pericarditis is likely, with a small effusion and no tamponade physiology. Obtain ECG, inflammatory markers, and troponin; review renal, bleeding, and medication risks; and start guideline-directed anti-inflammatory therapy with cardiology follow-up. Recurrent or refractory disease may require advanced imaging or targeted therapy.






Tip



Case format reminder: The case ends with a management decision, not just a diagnosis.

title: Module 4 — Pericardium
text:
Quiz






Note



Q1. On PLAX, you see an echo-free space posterior to the LV. How do you determine whether it is pericardial or pleural?






Caution





Answer Locate the descending thoracic aorta in cross-section near the left atrium. Pericardial fluid remains anterior to the descending aorta; left pleural fluid extends posterior to it.



Q2. A patient has a large effusion and is hypotensive. RV diastolic collapse is not clearly visible. What other findings support tamponade physiology?






Caution





Answer RA free-wall collapse, a plethoric IVC with reduced inspiratory collapse, exaggerated ventricular interdependence, a >25% inspiratory fall in mitral E-wave velocity, and a >40% inspiratory rise in tricuspid E-wave velocity support tamponade in spontaneous breathing. No single finding is required, and positive-pressure ventilation can alter the pattern.



Q3. You see an echogenic structure anterior to the RV. What is the most likely mimic, and how do you confirm it?






Caution





Answer Pericardial or epicardial fat. Confirm the speckled echogenic texture, anterior location, and motion with the heart. Compare multiple views and reduce gain. Free-flowing fluid may redistribute with position, but a loculated effusion may not.



Q4. The patient in Case 2 has metastatic cancer, progressive dyspnea, tachycardia, JVD, and a large effusion without definite chamber collapse. Does absent collapse make discharge safe?






Caution





Answer No. In this symptomatic patient, absent collapse alone does not establish safety. Obtain urgent comprehensive echo, monitored evaluation, and a specialist drainage plan. Collapse can be absent early or masked by elevated right-sided pressure. The effusion is cancer-associated with suspected malignant involvement; its etiology is not proven by the ultrasound.



Q5. Which features in acute pericarditis favor hospital evaluation?






Caution





Answer Fever >38°C, subacute course, large effusion (>20 mm), tamponade, failure of initial anti-inflammatory therapy, myocardial involvement, immunosuppression, trauma, and oral anticoagulant therapy favor hospital evaluation.



Q6. In traumatic tamponade, why is pericardiocentesis often insufficient?






Caution





Answer Traumatic hemopericardium may represent cardiac or great-vessel injury and can contain clot that will not drain through a needle or catheter. Pericardiocentesis may be only a bridge when surgery is not immediately available; definitive hemorrhage control usually requires operative repair.

section: 2. The four-question bedside echo in shock
text:
2. The four-question bedside echo in shock
A systematic framework for the undifferentiated hemodynamically unstable patient.
Every bedside echo in shock should answer these four questions, in this order:
1. Is there a pericardial effusion with tamponade physiology? If the clinical picture and echo support tamponade causing instability, activate definitive drainage immediately while continuing resuscitation. Drainage may require percutaneous or surgical treatment according to cause and anatomy. Isolated echo signs do not establish tamponade, and other causes of shock may coexist; see Module 4.
2. What is LV systolic function? Reduced EF identifies systolic dysfunction, not cardiac output or the dominant shock mechanism. A hyperdynamic LV can still have low stroke volume. Integrate forward flow, perfusion, loading, and the rest of the examination; see Module 2.
3. What is RV size and function? RV dilation and septal flattening suggest abnormal RV loading/function. Consider PE, ARDS, RV ischemia, chronic pulmonary hypertension, and acute-on-chronic disease. Low LV EF may coexist, but neither chamber appearance alone establishes the cause of shock; see Module 3.
4. What is the IVC? Interpret IVC diameter and respiration with ventilation, effort, and other right-sided findings. They can contribute to RA pressure assessment, but do not alone establish fluid responsiveness or tolerance. Use a suitable dynamic test and assess congestion; see Module 5.

text:
4. When findings conflict
The exam doesn’t always give you a clean answer.






Tip



Mixed shock state — reduced EF with small IVC; how to interpret and what to do.


Common conflicting scenarios and how to reason through them:
Reduced EF + small IVC Low EF and a small IVC do not establish either low output or a need for fluid. If hypoperfusion is present, assess responsiveness and tolerance with a suitable dynamic test. A small fluid challenge may be considered when underfilling is plausible and a response can be measured; stop if ineffective or congestion worsens. Support perfusion pressure and investigate the cause.
Hyperdynamic LV + plethoric IVC A hyperdynamic appearance does not prove high output. The IVC may reflect elevated RA pressure, ventilation, or other influences. Consider sepsis, RV disease, severe tricuspid regurgitation, and mixed states. Assess forward flow and congestion rather than assigning a mechanism from these two findings alone.
Normal LV + dilated RV + plethoric IVC (no effusion) Consider PE or ARDS-related cor pulmonale, but also RV infarction and chronic or acute-on-chronic PH. Avoid large empiric fluid loads in a distended, congested RV. Determine cause, severity, and perfusion needs before selecting afterload reduction or other therapy.
Large effusion + no tamponade physiology + plethoric IVC A large effusion and plethoric IVC may have several explanations. Absence of visible collapse does not exclude tamponade in every setting, including elevated right-sided pressures. Assess symptoms, perfusion, full echo findings, and etiology; do not assume two independent chronic problems from these signs alone.

title: Module 9 — Integration
text:
5. Serial exams and trending
Echo is not a one-time test.






Tip



Before/after comparison — echo before and after 1 L fluid bolus in a patient with septic shock.


The true power of bedside echo in critical care is the ability to perform serial exams and track the response to interventions in real time. Key scenarios for repeat assessment:

After a fluid bolus: Did IVC diameter change? Did cardiac output improve (visual or measured)? Did venous congestion worsen?
After vasopressor dose change: Did LV or RV filling improve?
After diuresis: Is venous congestion resolving? Is IVC size decreasing?
After pericardiocentesis: Is tamponade physiology resolved? Is there residual constrictive physiology?
Trending over hours: Is RV function improving with treatment of PE or ARDS? Is EF recovering in myocarditis?

Each exam should be compared to the prior exam, not interpreted in isolation. Document the key findings (EF category, RV:LV ratio, IVC diameter, IVC collapsibility) so that trends are visible across shifts.

title: Module 9 — Integration
text:
6. Integration cases
Complex cases requiring synthesis of all modules.


Case 1: The patient in undifferentiated shock
Clinical scenario: A 64-year-old man with no significant cardiac history is transferred from a community hospital with “septic shock, possible PE.” He has been on norepinephrine for 6 hours and received 5 L of crystalloid. On arrival: BP 74/48, HR 128, temp 37.8°C, O2 sat 90% on 6 L NC. He is slightly confused. Chest X-ray shows bilateral infiltrates. Troponin is mildly elevated.
Systematic four-question exam:






Tip






What you see: 1. No pericardial effusion. 2. LV severely reduced EF. Global hypokinesis, no RWMA. 3. RV moderately dilated. D-sign present. McConnell’s sign absent. TAPSE 14 mm. 4. IVC 2.5 cm, non-collapsing.
Integration: Biventricular systolic dysfunction and possible congestion may contribute to shock, but the scan does not establish cardiac output or exclude vasodilatory sepsis. Troponin can rise in several critical illnesses. Consider ischemia, myocarditis, sepsis-associated dysfunction, and acute-on-chronic disease. Bilateral opacities may reflect edema, infection, or both.
How does this change management? Pause further empiric fluid loading while assessing responsiveness and tolerance. Continue necessary vasopressor support, obtain ECG and urgent comprehensive echo, and assess forward flow/perfusion; consider advanced monitoring if uncertainty persists. Add an inotrope only when the hemodynamic indication is supported, including persistent hypoperfusion with cardiac dysfunction despite adequate volume and pressure. Continue evaluation and treatment of possible infection while investigating cardiac causes. Escalate to the shock/cardiology team and select coronary evaluation according to the ACS presentation.



Case 2: Post-arrest resuscitation — what caused the arrest?
Clinical scenario: A 58-year-old woman had a witnessed cardiac arrest in the hospital corridor. She was resuscitated in 8 minutes with 2 shocks and CPR. Now intubated, hemodynamically marginal on vasopressors. No prior cardiac history. The team wants to know: VF arrest from ACS, PE, or something else?
Systematic four-question exam:






Tip






What you see: 1. No effusion. 2. LV: anterior and apical wall akinesis. Severely reduced EF. No global hypokinesis — the inferior and lateral walls move. 3. RV: normal size. No D-sign. Normal TAPSE. 4. IVC: 2.0 cm, 30% collapse (borderline).
Integration: Regional wall motion abnormality in the anterior/LAD distribution with a normal RV. This is a large anterior STEMI causing VF arrest. The RV is not dilated — this is not a PE causing the arrest. The IVC is borderline, consistent with post-resuscitation state.
How does this change management? Activate the cath lab immediately for emergent PCI. This is STEMI-equivalent post-arrest — coronary angiography is indicated regardless of the post-resuscitation ECG. Initiate targeted temperature management per protocol. The echo finding of an anterior RWMA pointing to the LAD is the critical finding that directs the team to the right intervention.



Case 3: Hypoxic respiratory failure — cardiac or pulmonary?
Clinical scenario: A 71-year-old woman with COPD is admitted with progressive dyspnea over 3 days. She is hypoxic (O2 sat 84% on 10 L), hypotensive (BP 90/60), and has bilateral crackles and lower extremity edema. BNP is 1,800 pg/mL. Chest X-ray shows bilateral opacities. The team is debating whether to intubate for COPD exacerbation or initiate diuresis for decompensated heart failure.
Systematic four-question exam:






Tip






What you see: 1. No effusion. 2. LV: severely reduced EF, dilated — chronic appearance. 3. RV: moderately dilated. D-sign (diastolic flattening, consistent with volume overload). 4. IVC: 2.8 cm, non-collapsing. Hepatic veins dilated.
Integration: The findings support decompensated heart failure with congestion. Assess lung findings, gas exchange, and the clinical history to determine how much edema, COPD, infection, or another process contributes. The known diagnoses may coexist; EF and venous appearance do not independently identify the sole cause of respiratory failure.
How does this change management? Use NIV when appropriate for respiratory distress and treat supported congestion, with diuresis and blood-pressure management tailored to perfusion. Inotropes are reserved for a supported low-output/hypoperfusion indication rather than persistent low EF. Treat contributing COPD or infection when present. If intubation becomes necessary, base that decision on respiratory failure, airway protection, and trajectory while anticipating hemodynamic effects.



Case 4: The patient who “isn’t responding” to treatment
Clinical scenario: A 77-year-old man with known COPD and newly diagnosed lung cancer was admitted 3 days ago for presumed COPD exacerbation. He has been on bronchodilators, steroids, and antibiotics with minimal improvement. He remains hypoxic and increasingly vasopressor-dependent. Repeat echo is requested by the ICU attending.
Systematic four-question exam:






Tip






What you see: 1. Moderate pericardial effusion. No RA or RV collapse. IVC plethoric. 2. LV: normal EF. No RWMA. 3. RV: moderately dilated. D-sign present (pressure overload pattern — systolic flattening). 4. IVC: 2.4 cm, non-collapsing.
Integration: Two separate findings: a pericardial effusion (likely malignant) and RV pressure overload without tamponade physiology. The effusion is not causing tamponade. The RV dilation with pressure-overload D-sign in a patient with lung cancer raises the possibility of pulmonary hypertension from tumor invasion, PE, or extrinsic pulmonary vascular compression. Neither finding fits a primary COPD exacerbation.
How does this change management? CT pulmonary angiography to evaluate for PE and pulmonary vascular involvement by tumor. Oncology consultation for the effusion (malignant pericardial effusion likely). Reframe the clinical diagnosis — this is not a COPD exacerbation. The failure to respond to bronchodilators and steroids was a clue that the diagnosis was wrong.



Case 5: The post-operative patient who won’t come off the ventilator
Clinical scenario: A 69-year-old man undergoes elective aortic valve replacement. He is extubated on post-op day 2 but reintubated 6 hours later for respiratory failure. He is now post-op day 5, sedated, and failing repeated extubation trials. An ICU team requests bedside echo to evaluate hemodynamics.
Systematic four-question exam:






Tip



Loops for interpretation — post-surgical windows (often challenging).


What you see: 1. Small anterior effusion. No chamber collapse. 2. LV: EF 45% (mildly reduced, new compared to pre-op 60%). Anterior wall motion mildly reduced. 3. RV: mildly dilated. TAPSE 14 mm. 4. IVC: 2.2 cm, 20% distensibility during mechanical ventilation. This isolated measurement does not classify fluid responsiveness; interpret settings and patient effort and use a suitable dynamic test.
Integration: New LV dysfunction and a regional change raise concern for postoperative myocardial dysfunction or perioperative ischemia. They do not alone prove that cardiac dysfunction is causing failure to wean. Assess pulmonary mechanics, gas exchange, fluid balance/congestion, and perfusion alongside comprehensive echo. Postoperative annular motion can also affect TAPSE.
How does this change management? Obtain ECG and serial troponins and involve cardiology for comprehensive postoperative assessment. Evaluate both cardiac and pulmonary causes of weaning failure. Treat demonstrable congestion if perfusion allows, address rate/rhythm abnormalities, and use inotropic support only for an appropriate hemodynamic indication. Reassess physiology before the next extubation attempt; persistent low EF alone is not a treatment target.






Tip



Integration reminder: The power of the four-question exam is not in any single finding. It is in the composite picture and the management decision that follows.

title: Module 9 — Integration
text:
Quiz






Note



Q1. A patient in shock has a hyperdynamic LV, a dilated RV with D-sign, and a plethoric IVC. No pericardial effusion. What is the most likely hemodynamic phenotype and the priority intervention?






Caution





Answer Obstructive shock from pulmonary embolism (or acute cor pulmonale). The hyperdynamic LV is underfilled due to RV failure impairing output. The priority is reducing RV afterload — systemic anticoagulation, and in hemodynamic collapse, systemic thrombolytics or catheter-directed therapy. Do not give fluid boluses.



Q2. You find a severely reduced EF and a small, collapsible IVC in a hypotensive patient. What does this suggest and how do you manage it?






Caution





Answer These findings do not prove a cardiogenic/hypovolemic combination. Assess perfusion, forward flow, responsiveness, and tolerance. If underfilling is plausible, a measured small fluid challenge may help; stop if there is no meaningful benefit or congestion worsens. Support pressure as needed. Consider an inotrope for persistent hypoperfusion with cardiac dysfunction under appropriate loading and pressure conditions, not because EF fails to normalize.



Q3. After performing a bedside echo, you are unsure whether the reduced EF is new or chronic. How does the LV size help you distinguish?






Caution





Answer Dilation can support chronic remodeling, but does not exclude an acute insult. A nondilated LV can accompany several acute or chronic conditions. Compare prior imaging and assess symptoms, ECG, biomarkers, and perfusion. Urgency follows the syndrome: acute-on-chronic disease and myocarditis with shock can be immediately dangerous.



Q4. A patient has a normal-appearing LV, dilated RV with McConnell’s sign, and a plethoric IVC. What further information determines whether urgent PE reperfusion is appropriate?






Caution





Answer These findings raise concern for PE but do not establish it; RV ischemia and other RV disorders can mimic this pattern. Determine clinical probability, hemodynamic/respiratory stability, other RV pressure-overload signs, competing causes, and bleeding risk. With profound instability, high PE probability, no better explanation, and CT unsafe or unavailable, urgent reperfusion may be justified without CT through the PE response pathway. Otherwise pursue the appropriate diagnostic/risk assessment. A sonographic sign alone is not an indication for systemic thrombolysis.



Q5. What is the purpose of serial bedside echo in the ICU, and what should be documented to make serial exams useful?






Caution





Answer Serial echo tracks the response to interventions and identifies deterioration or recovery over time. A single exam is a snapshot; serial exams reveal trajectory. Document key quantitative or semi-quantitative findings at each exam: EF category (severely reduced / mildly reduced / normal / hyperdynamic), RV:LV ratio, IVC diameter and collapsibility, presence of chamber collapse or D-sign. This allows any clinician picking up the patient to immediately understand where the hemodynamics started and where they are now.

title: Module 9 — Abdominal Ultrasound
text:
What clinical question does this exam answer, and how do findings change management?






Note



The bedside decision frame: Four distinct questions, each with its own clinical trigger.

Is there intraperitoneal free fluid? In trauma, free fluid = blood until proven otherwise. In the non-trauma ICU patient, free fluid may represent ascites, hollow viscus perforation, or internal hemorrhage.
Is there a distended, obstructed bladder? Urinary retention is a common, painful, and easily treated problem — one that is frequently missed in sedated or altered patients.
Is there hydronephrosis? Ureteral obstruction causing hydronephrosis may explain AKI, flank pain, or urosepsis in an undrained system.
In the trauma patient — is there free fluid in the pericardium? The subxiphoid FAST view incorporates cardiac assessment (see Module 1).



Abdominal ultrasound at the bedside is fast, non-invasive, and immediately actionable. The FAST exam (Focused Assessment with Sonography in Trauma) is the standard of care in trauma resuscitation. In non-trauma critical care, bladder and kidney assessment are high-yield applications that require minimal additional training.

text:
2. Image acquisition
Probe, windows, and technique for this module.
Use a curvilinear (low-frequency, 2–5 MHz) probe for all abdominal windows — the penetration depth required for the liver, spleen, kidneys, and pelvis exceeds what a linear probe provides. A phased array probe is an acceptable substitute for FAST but is less ideal for the pelvic view.
Machine preset: Abdominal. Adjust depth to see structures of interest with adequate margin.


Right upper quadrant — Morrison’s pouch






Tip



RUQ acquisition — hepatorenal interface, fan through Morrison’s pouch, assess for free fluid.


Probe placement: Probe in the right mid-axillary line, 8th–11th intercostal space, indicator toward the patient’s head. Fan through the hepatorenal interface (Morrison’s pouch) — the potential space between the liver and right kidney.
What you are looking for: Any anechoic (black) stripe between the liver and right kidney. In a normal exam, the liver and kidney appear to be in direct contact with a thin hyperechoic stripe of Gerota’s fascia between them. Free fluid appears as a wedge or stripe of anechoic material in the dependent hepatorenal space. Also assess the inferior tip of the liver and the right paracolic gutter.
Pearls: Morrison’s pouch is the most dependent intraperitoneal space in the supine position and the most sensitive location for detecting free fluid. As little as 100–200 mL of free fluid may be visible here.



Left upper quadrant — splenorenal space






Tip



LUQ acquisition — splenorenal interface, subphrenic space, left paracolic gutter.


Probe placement: Left posterior axillary line, 8th–11th intercostal space, indicator toward the head. This window is more posterior than the RUQ view — a common error is imaging too anteriorly and missing the spleen.
What you are looking for: Free fluid between the spleen and left kidney (splenorenal space), and in the subphrenic space (between the diaphragm and spleen). A left pleural effusion appears above the diaphragm — do not confuse it with subphrenic free fluid. The diaphragm is the landmark: fluid above = pleural, fluid below = peritoneal.
Pearls: The LUQ is less sensitive than the RUQ because the splenorenal space is less dependent. Free fluid may not accumulate here until larger volumes are present. Assess the subphrenic and paracolic regions thoroughly.



Suprapubic — pelvis






Tip



Suprapubic acquisition — bladder as acoustic window, free fluid in the pouch of Douglas (female) or rectovesical space (male), transverse and sagittal planes.


Probe placement: Suprapubic, just above the symphysis pubis, indicator to the patient’s right (transverse) or head (sagittal). The bladder serves as an acoustic window to the posterior pelvic structures.
What you are looking for: Free fluid posterior to the bladder (pouch of Douglas in females, rectovesical space in males). In females, look for fluid in the cul-de-sac posterior to the uterus. Scan in both transverse and sagittal planes. Free fluid appears anechoic, dependent, and irregular in shape.
Bladder assessment: See dedicated section below.
Pearls: The pelvic view requires a full or at least partially full bladder to serve as an acoustic window. In patients who are oliguric or have been catheterized, the pelvic view may be limited. The pelvic space is the most dependent location in the erect position — significant fluid may accumulate here even when the upper quadrants appear negative.



Subxiphoid — pericardium and cardiac
Covered in Module 1. The subxiphoid view is the fourth standard FAST window.



Bladder — transverse and sagittal






Tip



Bladder assessment — full bladder as an anechoic structure, volume estimation, wall assessment.


Probe placement: Suprapubic, transverse then sagittal. The bladder appears as a well-defined anechoic structure posterior to the symphysis. Measure three dimensions: transverse (width), anteroposterior (depth), and craniocaudal (height). Bladder volume (mL) ≈ 0.52 × width × depth × height (in cm). Some machines calculate this automatically.
Significant residual volume: >300 mL post-void, or a distended bladder in a patient with reduced consciousness who is not catheterized.



Kidneys — longitudinal






Tip



Right and left kidney — normal cortex and collecting system vs hydronephrosis grades.


Probe placement: Coronal plane, similar to FAST views but oriented to the kidneys. Right kidney: right mid-axillary line, indicator up. Left kidney: left posterior axillary line, indicator up. Obtain a longitudinal image of the entire kidney — cortex, medullary pyramids, and collecting system (renal pelvis and calyces).
What you are looking for: Any separation of the renal sinus (echogenic central collecting system) by anechoic fluid — indicating hydronephrosis.

title: Module 9 — Abdominal Ultrasound
text:
3. Normal & normal variants






Tip



Normal FAST exam — no free fluid at each window. Normal kidney. Normal bladder.



Normal FAST exam
No anechoic fluid in Morrison’s pouch, splenorenal space, or pelvis. The subxiphoid view shows no pericardial effusion. Organ surfaces are in direct contact with each other and with the abdominal wall.


Normal kidney
Length 9–12 cm, width 4–6 cm. The renal cortex is slightly less echogenic than the liver. The renal sinus (collecting system) appears as a central echogenic structure without internal fluid. Medullary pyramids appear as hypoechoic triangular structures pointing toward the sinus.


Normal bladder
Thin-walled, smooth, anechoic. Wall thickness <3 mm when full. Urine is anechoic; debris, clots, or calculi appear as echogenic foci within the lumen.


Perihepatic fat and ascites mimics
Small amounts of fat around the liver and mesentery can mimic minimal free fluid. Fat has a characteristic echogenicity (not purely anechoic) and does not layer into dependent spaces the way free fluid does. Bowel loops with fluid should not be mistaken for free fluid — identify peristalsis and bowel wall to distinguish.

title: Module 9 — Abdominal Ultrasound
text:
4. Pathology library
Organized by finding.

Free fluid — traumatic (hemoperitoneum)






Tip




Anechoic free fluid in Morrison’s pouch
Moderate-large free fluid in the pelvis
Echogenic free fluid — acute blood



In trauma, any free fluid is assumed to be blood. Acute hemoperitoneum may be anechoic (early, not clotted) or echogenic (clotted blood). The pattern and volume guide management.
Grading by volume and distribution:








Finding
Estimated Volume
Management Implication




Trace fluid in Morrison’s pouch only
<250 mL
Serial exam, reassess


Fluid in RUQ + pelvis
500–1000 mL
Operative vs non-operative decision based on hemodynamics


Fluid in all three windows
>1000 mL
Likely operative in hemodynamically unstable patient



Teaching points:

A positive FAST in a hemodynamically unstable patient = OR, not CT. Do not delay operative intervention for imaging.
A negative FAST does not rule out intraperitoneal injury — solid organ injuries may be present without free fluid early.
A positive FAST in a hemodynamically stable patient allows CT for better injury characterization before operative decision.
Echogenic (bright) free fluid = acute blood/clot. Anechoic free fluid in trauma = blood (until proven otherwise), even if it looks like simple fluid.




Free fluid — non-traumatic






Tip



Ascites — large volume anechoic free fluid surrounding bowel loops, “floating” bowel.


In the non-trauma ICU patient, free fluid may represent: - Ascites: Cirrhosis, malignancy, heart failure — anechoic, often massive, bowel loops appear to float - Ruptured viscus: Bowel perforation — complex, echogenic, or mixed fluid - Ruptured ectopic pregnancy: Pelvic free fluid in a woman of childbearing age = ectopic until proven otherwise - Internal hemorrhage: Post-procedural, anticoagulated, aortic aneurysm rupture
Teaching points:

In a non-trauma patient with hypotension and pelvic free fluid, always check a urine or serum beta-hCG before attributing fluid to another cause.
Ruptured ectopic with free fluid and hemodynamic instability = emergent gynecologic surgery.
Large ascites can be drained under ultrasound guidance (see Module 11).




Urinary retention and bladder assessment






Tip




Massively distended bladder — large anechoic structure filling the pelvis
Bladder volume calculation with three-plane measurement



A distended bladder (>300 mL post-void residual) in a patient with reduced consciousness, confusion, agitation, or unexplained pain is urinary retention until proven otherwise.
Teaching points:

Urinary retention is common in the ICU — opioids, anticholinergics, and sedatives all reduce detrusor function.
In a male patient with an enlarged prostate, any acute illness may precipitate retention.
A fully distended bladder (>500–800 mL) can reflexively inhibit cardiac output and worsen hemodynamics.
Treatment is urethral or suprapubic catheterization. Ultrasound-guided suprapubic catheterization is appropriate when urethral access is not possible.
Post-decompression diuresis can occur after relief of chronic obstruction — anticipate and replace fluids.




Hydronephrosis






Tip




Grade 1 hydronephrosis — mild dilation of the renal pelvis only
Grade 2 — dilation of pelvis and calyces, preserved cortex
Grade 3 — severe dilation, thinned cortex



Hydronephrosis is dilation of the renal collecting system from ureteral obstruction. It appears as anechoic fluid within the renal sinus, separating the echogenic collecting system walls.
Grading:



Grade
Appearance




1 (mild)
Pelvis dilated, calyces normal


2 (moderate)
Pelvis and calyces dilated, cortex preserved


3 (severe)
Marked dilation, cortex thinned



Teaching points:

Hydronephrosis in a patient with AKI = obstructive nephropathy until proven otherwise. Relieve the obstruction (Foley, ureteral stent, nephrostomy) before attributing the AKI to another cause.
Bilateral hydronephrosis = bilateral obstruction or bladder outlet obstruction (BPH, mass). Check the bladder first.
Hydronephrosis + fever = obstructed, infected system (pyonephrosis) — urgent drainage is required (not just antibiotics).
Normal ultrasound does not rule out obstruction in early or acute cases — the collecting system may not have had time to dilate.

title: Module 9 — Abdominal Ultrasound
text:
5. Integration cases
Cases where the finding changes management.


Case 1: Trauma — positive FAST in a hypotensive patient
Clinical scenario: A 25-year-old man is brought in after a motor vehicle collision at highway speed. He is hypotensive (BP 78/50) and tachycardic (HR 132) on arrival. GCS is 14. The trauma team is assembled.
What exam would you perform? Immediate FAST exam as part of the primary survey.






Tip








What you see: Morrison’s pouch: free fluid, moderate volume. Splenorenal space: free fluid. Pelvis: large volume free fluid. Subxiphoid: no pericardial effusion.
How does this change management? Positive FAST with hemodynamic instability = operative intervention. Do not take this patient to CT. Transfuse blood products in a 1:1:1 ratio (PRBC:FFP:platelets) as a bridge to the OR. Activate massive transfusion protocol. The trauma surgeon takes over — the bedside echo has already answered the most important question.



Case 2: Urosepsis with flank pain — is the system obstructed?
Clinical scenario: A 70-year-old man with a history of kidney stones presents with fever (39.2°C), right flank pain, and hypotension. UA shows pyuria. He is started on IV antibiotics and fluids. The team is wondering if he needs urgent urologic intervention.
What exam would you perform? Renal ultrasound — bilateral kidneys.






Tip






What you see: Right kidney: grade 2–3 hydronephrosis. Echogenic material within the dilated collecting system (debris). Left kidney: normal.
How does this change management? Obstructed, infected right kidney — pyonephrosis. Antibiotics alone are insufficient. Emergent urology consultation for urgent drainage — either ureteral stent or percutaneous nephrostomy. Septic shock from an obstructed system will not resolve without drainage. This is a surgical emergency, not a medical one.



Case 3: Altered mental status and agitation — is this retention?
Clinical scenario: A 77-year-old man with BPH, on post-op day 1 following a hip replacement, is increasingly agitated and confused. Vitals are stable. He received significant opioids intraoperatively. His Foley was removed 4 hours ago.
What exam would you perform? Bladder ultrasound.






Tip






What you see: Distended, smooth-walled bladder. Estimated volume 680 mL.
How does this change management? Urinary retention causing agitation and delirium in a post-operative elderly male. Replace the urethral catheter. Agitation should resolve within minutes of bladder decompression. Avoid sedatives — they will worsen delirium without treating the cause. Monitor for post-obstructive diuresis. Address BPH pharmacologically (alpha-blocker) before the next void trial.



Case 4: Ruptured ectopic pregnancy
Clinical scenario: A 28-year-old woman presents to the ED with sudden-onset lower abdominal pain and presyncope. BP 90/60, HR 118. She reports her last menstrual period was 7 weeks ago. She thought she might be pregnant but has not confirmed it.
What exam would you perform? FAST exam with attention to the pelvic view, and immediate beta-hCG.






Tip







What you see: Large volume of free fluid in the pelvis and RUQ. No intrauterine pregnancy visible. Echogenic mass adjacent to the left ovary. Beta-hCG returns at 4,200 mIU/mL.
How does this change management? Ruptured ectopic pregnancy with hemoperitoneum. This is a surgical emergency. Call OB/GYN for emergent surgical intervention. Two large-bore IVs, blood type and crossmatch, activate the OR. Do not perform a diagnostic laparoscopy — this patient needs a therapeutic laparotomy or laparoscopy. Time is critical.






Tip



Case format reminder: The case ends with a management decision, not just a diagnosis.

title: Module 9 — Abdominal Ultrasound
text:
Quiz






Note



Q1. Where is the most sensitive location for detecting free fluid in a supine patient, and why?






Caution





Answer Morrison’s pouch (the hepatorenal space in the right upper quadrant) is the most sensitive location because it is the most dependent intraperitoneal space in the supine patient. Fluid accumulates there preferentially due to gravity. As little as 100–200 mL of free fluid may be visible at this location before it is detectable elsewhere.



Q2. A FAST exam is negative in a hemodynamically stable trauma patient with abdominal tenderness. What is the next step?






Caution





Answer A negative FAST does not rule out solid organ injury or retroperitoneal injury. In a stable patient with abdominal tenderness and a mechanism concerning for injury, CT of the abdomen and pelvis with IV contrast is the next step. CT has much higher sensitivity than ultrasound for detecting solid organ lacerations that have not yet bled into the peritoneum.



Q3. You detect hydronephrosis in a patient with new AKI. What is the next clinical question?






Caution





Answer Is the obstruction bilateral or unilateral? Bilateral hydronephrosis (or hydronephrosis in a solitary kidney) explains AKI — the obstruction must be relieved urgently. Unilateral hydronephrosis alone does not explain AKI unless the contralateral kidney is absent or non-functional. Also ask: is there fever or signs of infection? If so, the obstructed system is infected (pyonephrosis) and requires emergent drainage, not just observation.



Q4. A left pleural effusion appears as fluid above the diaphragm on the LUQ view. How do you distinguish it from subphrenic free fluid?






Caution





Answer The diaphragm is the key landmark — it appears as a bright echogenic curved line. Pleural fluid is above the diaphragm (between the lung and the diaphragm). Peritoneal free fluid is below the diaphragm (in the subphrenic or splenorenal space). The “mirror artifact” — a mirror image of the spleen or liver appearing above the diaphragm — is a normal artifact in the absence of pleural fluid. The presence of a true anechoic collection above the diaphragm that does not show the mirror artifact indicates a pleural effusion.



Q5. Why is pelvic free fluid in a woman of reproductive age a critical finding that requires immediate additional testing?






Caution





Answer Pelvic free fluid in a reproductive-age woman must be evaluated for ruptured ectopic pregnancy — a life-threatening condition that can produce rapid exsanguination. A urine or serum beta-hCG must be obtained immediately. If beta-hCG is positive and there is no intrauterine pregnancy on ultrasound, ruptured ectopic is highly likely until proven otherwise. Hemodynamic instability with pelvic free fluid and a positive beta-hCG = emergent surgical intervention, not further imaging.
